docs.title: FieldNeuroToolbox (FNT)
docs.text:
Preprocessing and analysis toolbox for field and laboratory neurobehavioral data. FNT is open source and free for research and hobby use. It is released as-is and grows alongside our own research.

Bugs and feature requests: please open an issue.

docs.title: What's inside
docs.text:
FNT bundles GUI tools for the common data types of field and laboratory neuroethology, in one desktop app that runs on an ordinary laptop:

  • Audio / USV

    Ultrasonic vocalization detection, classification and audio preprocessing, including the Classic Audio Detector (CAD).

  • Mask Audio Detector (MAD)

    Label calls on the spectrogram with SAM, train a segmentation model, and run it over thousands of recordings.

  • Video Processing

    Batch preprocessing, trimming, concatenation and manual behavioral scoring.

  • Video Tracking

    SAM-based interactive animal tracking for behavioral assays.

  • Mask Tracker

    Label animals with SAM, train a YOLO segmentation model, review its predictions and run it over whole videos.

  • UWB Tracking

    Ultra-wideband positions to cleaned, smoothed tracks, contact bouts, chases and region occupancy.

  • RFID Tracking

    Biomark reader downloads to cleaned reads, bouts, zone holders and co-occupancy, with QC reports.

  • Imaging

    Zeiss CZI microscopy viewing, processing and cell quantification.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
The easiest way to use FNT is the pre-built standalone executable; no Python or Anaconda is needed.

  1. Download the latest release for your OS from the Releases page.
  2. Extract the archive.
  3. Run the fnt executable.

See Installation for the standalone requirements (ffmpeg) and for the development installation if you want to modify the code.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: There are two ways to run FNT: the pre-built standalone executable (recommended for most users) or a development installation (if you want to modify the code).

docs.title: Standalone Executable (Recommended)
docs.text: You do not need to install Python or Anaconda for this version.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • ffmpeg — must be installed and on your system PATH for audio/video features. On Windows, see Installing ffmpeg on Windows below.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Download the latest release .zip or .tar.gz for your OS from the Releases page.
  2. Extract the archive.
  3. Run the extracted fnt executable to launch the GUI.

macOS security permission

Since the executable is unsigned, macOS Gatekeeper will block it. Open Terminal and run xattr -cr path/to/fnt on the extracted file (drag it from Finder into Terminal to paste the path). This removes the quarantine attribute from the executable and its bundled dependencies.

Windows SmartScreen

You may see a "Windows protected your PC" warning. Click More info → Run anyway.

docs.title: Development Installation
docs.text: Use this method if you intend to modify the code or prefer managing your own Python environment.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Git on the command line (on your PATH). Installing GitHub Desktop alone is not sufficient — it bundles a git that isn't exposed to the terminal. The steps below install git into the conda environment.
  • Anaconda or Miniconda
  • Python 3.12 or newer (3.13 recommended; the codebase uses 3.12+ syntax)
  • ffmpeg — required for audio/video processing. Not a pip dependency, so pip install -e . alone does not provide it.

docs.title: Installing ffmpeg on Windows
docs.text:
Do not use conda install ffmpeg on Windows

The conda-forge ffmpeg package on Windows has a known DLL conflict (libintl / gdk-pixbuf / fontconfig) that causes it to crash during install and at runtime. Install ffmpeg system-wide instead.

  1. Download the "release essentials" zip from gyan.dev/ffmpeg/builds.
  2. Extract it to a permanent location, e.g. C:\ffmpeg.
  3. Add the bin folder (e.g. C:\ffmpeg\bin) to your system PATH: Settings → System → About → Advanced system settings → Environment Variables → Path → New.
  4. Open a new terminal and verify: ffmpeg -version.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/calebvogt/fnt.git
conda create --name fnt python=3.13
conda activate fnt
conda install git -y
cd path\to\fnt
pip install -e .

(ffmpeg is installed system-wide per the section above — do not conda install ffmpeg.)

docs.title: macOS / Linux
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/calebvogt/fnt.git
conda create --name fnt python=3.13
conda activate fnt
conda install git -y
conda install -c conda-forge ffmpeg -y
cd path/to/fnt
pip install -e .

On macOS/Linux the conda-forge ffmpeg package works fine.

docs.title: Launch the GUI
docs.text:
conda activate fnt
fnt

docs.title: GPU Support (Optional)
docs.text:
For SAM-based video tracking, the Mask Tracker and MAD training and inference, a GPU is a large speedup. Install PyTorch with CUDA support. The right command depends on your NVIDIA driver: MAD's Help ▸ Check GPU / CUDA setup… prints the exact pip command for your machine, or pick one on pytorch.org. For example, for CUDA 12.6:

conda activate fnt
pip install torch torchvision --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu126

Verify GPU detection:

python -c "import torch; print('CUDA available:', torch.cuda.is_available())"

This requires an NVIDIA GPU with CUDA support. Tools run on CPU otherwise, but significantly slower.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text:
Because the package is installed in editable mode:

cd path/to/fnt
git pull

If the update changed pyproject.toml (new dependencies), re-run the install:

conda activate fnt
pip install -e .

docs.title: FED3 v3: device rule, schedules and protocol files
docs.text: [!WARNING] Draft. Nothing here is implemented yet. This document is the contract between three pieces that will be built against it: the FED3 firmware (fnt-fed3, v3), the FNT protocol compiler and run monitor, and the FNT FED tab. There is no compatibility with the legacy FED3 library's modes, commands or file format.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
Run FED3 devices unattended for weeks, in single-device and multi-device (competitive, social) arrangements, with behaviour defined in a file rather than in firmware.

  1. No new firmware for new combinations. A "mode" is a set of values for one configurable rule. Firmware changes only to add a new building block.
  2. The device runs the whole experiment. At Start, FNT compiles the protocol into a schedule for each device and uploads it. The device then makes:
  3. every per-poke decision;
  4. every phase change, whether time-, clock- or count-based;
  5. every dispense and every cue.

It keeps its schedule and its place in it on the SD card. A crashed, rebooted or unplugged PC changes nothing. 3. The PC watches, records and edits. FNT shows what each device is doing, keeps a live copy of the data, keeps the clocks set, and uploads a new schedule when the protocol is edited mid-run. It also checks the few conditions that depend on more than one device. 4. The SD card is the record. Every row the device writes is also sent live, numbered, and can be re-read after a gap. FNT's copy is byte-identical. 5. Every state can be rebuilt from what is on the card. After a power cut, watchdog reset or clock loss, the device works out where it should be, in the same way every time.

Concern Owner If the PC is down Poke decisions, ratio, timeout, quota Device Unaffected Dispensing, jam recovery, cues Device Unaffected Phase changes on time, clock time, rewards or pokes Device Unaffected Schedule and place in it Device, on SD Survive reboot and watchdog reset Phase changes that depend on several devices; manual advance FNT Wait until FNT returns, or take the phase's device-local fallback Run record SD; FNT copies it Rows are re-read on reconnect; nothing is lost Problems (jams, resets, offline devices) FNT shows them on screen Seen at the daily check once FNT is back; the rows are still on the card

docs.title: Terms
docs.text: Term Meaning Reward A met ratio. It delivers a pellet unless reward=none. Pellet A pellet that physically reached the well: earned, free-fed or dispensed by hand. Poke Any beam break of either poke, whatever its outcome.

docs.title: Part 1: the rule
docs.text: Each phase sets every key below. Any key a phase doesn't mention takes its default, not its value from the previous phase, so a phase always means the same thing wherever it is in the schedule.

docs.title: Keys
docs.text:
Key Values Default Meaning active left right both none left Which poke can earn a reward. count shared per_port shared With active=both: shared means pokes on either side add to one ratio counter; per_port gives each side its own. ratio 1–999 1 Pokes per reward, for fixed and random. ratio_kind fixed random progressive fixed random: each counted poke is rewarded with probability 1/ratio. progressive: the requirement after k rewards this phase is round(5·e^(0.2·(k+1)) − 5), giving 1, 2, 4, 6, 9, 12, 15, 20, 25, 32 and so on. ratio is ignored. timeout seconds, 0–3600 0 After a reward, pokes are logged with outcome timeout and do not count. min_poke_ms 0–5000 0 Pokes shorter than this are logged with outcome short and do not count. reward pellet none pellet none means a met ratio is logged and cued but delivers nothing. Use it for extinction, and with a bnc cue for opto self-stimulation. quota 0–9999 0 The most rewards per quota period (0 means unlimited). Once the quota is used up the patch is depleted: pokes are logged with outcome depleted and cue.depleted plays. quota_period seconds 0 0 means once per phase. Otherwise the quota refills every period, counted from when the phase started. free_feed 0 1 0 Keep a pellet in the well regardless of pokes. Pokes are still logged. refill_delay seconds 5 With free_feed: the wait after a retrieval before the next dispense.

How a poke is decided - A poke is decided the moment the beam breaks, so cues and dispenses have no delay. With min_poke_ms, it is decided once the beam has stayed broken that long, or as short if it is released sooner. - Its row is written when the beam is released, stamped with the time it broke and carrying its duration. A dispense that lands while the animal is still in the poke can therefore appear before the poke's row; time and ms keep the true order. A beam held longer than 60 s is logged as held at 60 s. - The first of these that applies is the outcome: 1. short: released before min_poke_ms; 2. pellet_in_well: a pellet is in the well or on its way; 3. inactive: not the active poke (with active=none, every poke); 4. timeout; 5. depleted; 6. reward if this poke meets the ratio, otherwise counted. - Every poke counts toward phase_left/phase_right and the pokes end condition, whatever its outcome.

Counting rules - A ratio counter resets to zero when it earns a reward (with per_port, only that side's counter), and all counters reset at a phase change. - Daily windows (Part 2) change keys but never reset counters.

Dispensing and jams - A dispense takes about a second, until the pellet breaks the well beam, which writes a dispense row. Taking it writes a retrieve row. - If the motor can't deliver a pellet, a jam row is written and the same dispense is retried every 10 minutes until it succeeds. A pellet fed by hand (FEED) isn't retried: nobody is owed it, and on the bench a retry would run the motor every 10 minutes on an empty hopper. At most one dispense is ever owed, so rewards earned while jammed don't pile up.

A blank or corrupt card boots into a one-phase schedule of the defaults: FR1, left poke, no cues.

docs.title: Cues
docs.text:
The lights are off unless a cue flashes them. A cue is up to 3 actions joined by +, played at once and without blocking. A new action on the same output replaces the one already playing. Every cue is triggered by a poke.

Key Plays when cue.reward A ratio is met (just before the dispense). cue.counted A counted poke has not yet met the ratio. cue.inactive The poke that cannot earn a reward is used. cue.timeout A poke is made during the timeout. cue.depleted A poke is made while the patch is depleted. Action Syntax Notes Tone tone:<hz>:<ms> A piezo square wave. One tone at a time, and there is no volume control. Click click Short for tone:800:8. Noise noise:<ms> A burst of random 50–250 Hz tones. It doesn't block. Flash flash:<target>:<r:g:b:w>:<ms> Target is bar (the 8-LED strip), poke_l, poke_r, pokes, or poke, meaning the poke that triggered the cue. The LEDs go dark again afterwards. BNC pulse train bnc:<width_ms>:<hz>:<count> For external speakers, LEDs, opto or sync.

none (the default for every cue) plays nothing.

docs.title: What replaces the old modes
docs.text:
Old mode Rule FR n ratio=n PR ratio_kind=progressive RR n ratio_kind=random ratio=n FRTO n, t s ratio=n timeout=t Free feeding active=none free_feed=1 Extinction reward=none Opto reward=none cue.reward=bnc:25:20:20 Any _R variant the same, plus active=right Timed feeding A phase with a daily window that sets free_feed=1 (example 3). Light tracking Dropped. It needs a poke light that stays on.

Each old mode's tone and light becomes a cue.reward choice.

docs.title: Part 2: device schedules
docs.text:
FNT compiles the protocol file (Part 4) into one schedule per device. It is plain text, one directive per line. The device keeps only the current phase in memory and reads the next phase from the card when it moves on, so a schedule's length costs SD space, not RAM.

Limits: at most 256 phases, 8 daily windows per phase, 6 until lines per phase, and 64 KB per schedule.

NAME Four-patch competition
PHASE Habituation
UNTIL at=19:00 day=3
SET active=none free_feed=1
PHASE Training
UNTIL goto
UNTIL after=345600
SET active=both cue.reward=tone:4000:200+flash:bar:0:30:0:0:1000 cue.depleted=click
PHASE Competition 1
UNTIL at=19:00
SET active=both quota=30 quota_period=3600 cue.reward=tone:4000:200+flash:bar:0:30:0:0:1000
SET cue.depleted=click
…
  • PHASE <name> starts a phase. Names can be up to 24 characters, and phases are numbered from 0 in file order.
  • SET <k=v …> gives the phase's rule and cues. One phase can have several SET lines. The compiler writes only keys that differ from their defaults, in the order of Part 1's tables. It starts a new SET line before any line passes 100 characters, so every upload line fits the 128-byte input limit. The same protocol therefore always compiles to the same text and the same crc.
  • WINDOW <hh:mm>-<hh:mm> <k=v …> overrides keys between two clock times every day. A window may cross midnight. Several WINDOW lines with the same times form one window, so long windows split the same way as SET.
  • UNTIL <condition> ends the phase. If there are several, the first one met ends it. A phase with no UNTIL runs until the run ends.

Every device in a run gets the same list of phases: the same count, the same names and the same order. Only the rules differ between devices. That keeps phase numbers meaningful across devices, for GOTO and for display.

Condition Ends the phase after=<s> That many seconds after the phase started. at=<hh:mm> At the first such clock time strictly after the phase started, so a phase that begins at 19:00 runs to 19:00 the next day. at=<hh:mm> day=<n> At that time on day n of the run. Day 1 is the calendar day of t0. rewards=<n> After n rewards in this phase. pokes=<n> side=<left\|right\|any> After n pokes of any outcome in this phase. goto Only when FNT sends GOTO. Used for manual advance and conditions that need FNT.

docs.title: Phase start times
docs.text:
Every later time condition counts from a phase's start time, so that time is defined exactly:

The phase was entered by Its start time is A time condition (after, at) The time the condition came due, not the time the device noticed. A count condition The time of the poke that met it. GOTO The time GOTO arrived. RUN:BEGIN t0.

Counting from the due time is what makes catching up exact. If the device is off when a time condition comes due, it boots and finds the condition already past, so: 1. it ends the phase at the due time and starts the next phase at that same time; 2. it checks the next phase the same way, and repeats until it reaches the present; 3. it logs each change as a phase row. The row is stamped when it is written, so timestamps never run backwards, and its detail records the phase's real start: Rot 2;catch-up;start=2026-10-22T19:00:00-07:00.

The device ends up in the same phase, with the same start time, as if it had never been off. Devices on a daily rotation therefore stay in step through outages.

Count conditions can't come due while a device is off, and goto waits for FNT.

docs.title: Clock
docs.text:
The device clock runs on standard time all year, with no daylight-saving changes. Every at time, window and day boundary uses it, and every row's timestamp carries its UTC offset (for example 2026-11-03T19:00:04-07:00).

That way: - a 19:00 phase change stays at the same point in a vivarium light cycle that ignores daylight saving; - the data never repeats or skips an hour.

FNT shows clock times, plots and the timeline in the same standard time, labelled with the zone. A vivarium whose lights do follow daylight saving would need daylight-saving rules in the firmware; that isn't planned until someone needs it.

Protection against clock problems

Problem What the device does The clock lost power (the RTC reports lostPower()) Status reports clock=unset. The device keeps the current phase's rule but ignores windows and time conditions until the clock is set. FNT sets it automatically as soon as it sees clock=unset, then the device catches up. A time change of more than 10 minutes during a run Refused with ERR,TIME_JUMP. FNT asks you to confirm and then sends TIME!:. This stops a mistyped clock from catching up through a week of phases. Small corrections from automatic sync Applied, and logged as a clock row showing the before and after times.

docs.title: State on the card, and recovery after a reboot
docs.text:
File Contents Written DEVICE.TXT Device number and the clock's UTC offset. On ID: and TIME:. SCHED.TXT The schedule in force. On upload during a run, and at RUN:BEGIN. NEXT.TXT A schedule uploaded outside a run, waiting for RUN:BEGIN. On upload outside a run. RUN.TXT Run id, t0, data file, ended flag, current phase number and phase start time. At RUN:BEGIN and RUN:END, and at each phase change. <run id>.CSV The run's rows. Before the first run ever, rows go to IDLE.CSV. Every event.

Every file except the data file is written to a temporary name and then renamed, so a power cut leaves either the old version or the new one, never a partial file.

On boot, the device rebuilds its state like this:

What Where it comes from Phase and its start time RUN.TXT Totals and phase counts the last row of the data file Quota used in the current period phase_rewards if quota_period=0; otherwise a scan back through rows to the start of the period, which is bounded by the period Partial progress towards a ratio Not kept: the ratio counter restarts at 0, and the boot row says so

It then catches up as described above.

After RUN:END the device stays in its current phase, including its daily windows, so timed feeding keeps working. No more phase changes happen, and the device keeps logging to the same data file until the next RUN:BEGIN.

docs.title: Part 3: serial commands (firmware v3)
docs.text: These are newline-terminated ASCII lines at 115200 baud. - Input lines can be up to 128 bytes. - Every device line is TYPE, followed by comma-separated key=value fields, except ROW, which carries an SD row verbatim. - ERR,<code>,<detail>: the detail is the rest of the line and may contain commas. - A command that writes rows sends them before its reply, so ROW lines can arrive between a command and its answer. - Every command that changes state is safe to repeat, except FEED: sending it twice has the same effect as sending it once, so FNT can always retry after a timeout. A repeated RUN:BEGIN for the run already in progress changes nothing.

docs.title: Host → device
docs.text:
Command Reply Purpose PING PONG,id=<n>,fw=3.0,proto=3 Discovery. FNT refuses proto ≠ 3. STATUS STATUS,… (below) Full state. FNT polls it every 30 s. TIME:<iso with offset> TIME,before=<iso>,after=<iso> Set the clock and its UTC offset. During a run a jump over 10 min is refused with ERR,TIME_JUMP; TIME!: overrides that. ID:<n> ID,id=<n> Set and save the ID (1-999), as the boot menu does: hold both pokes while FED3 ID shows at power-on, then left −1, right +1, saved after 4 s idle. Not offered during a run or after a watchdog restart. SCHED:BEGIN OK Start receiving a schedule. S:<line> OK or ERR,SCHED,<line no>,<reason> One schedule line, checked as it arrives. SCHED:COMMIT,<crc>[,<phase>] SCHED,crc=<hex>,phases=<n>,slot=<now\|next> Commit the upload (see below). RUN:BEGIN,<run_id>,<t0 iso>,<crc> RUN,run=<id>,file=<name>,phase=0 Start a run (see below). RUN:END RUN,run=<id>,ended=1 Log run_end. Phase changes stop; the current phase and its windows continue (Part 2). GOTO:<from>,<to> PHASE,n=<to>,name=<name> Move from phase from to phase to. Ignored with ERR,GOTO_STALE if the device is no longer in from, so a delayed or repeated GOTO can't skip a phase or move a device backwards. READ:<run_id>,<from_seq> ROW,… lines, then READ_END,run=<id>,last=<seq> Re-send rows from from_seq onward. These interleave safely with live rows. FEED FEED,result=<started\|pellet_in_well\|jam> Dispense once by hand. The outcome follows as a dispense (detail=manual) or jam row. Counts as a pellet but not a reward. TEST:<cue> OK Play a cue with the same syntax as cue.*. LIGHTS:on, LIGHTS:off LIGHTS,on=<0\|1> The bar and both pokes white and steady, to find a device on the bench (firmware 3.1). Cues flash over them. Off at boot and at RUN:BEGIN, so a run never starts lit. REBOOT (the device restarts) Remote recovery; a BOOT line follows.

SCHED:COMMIT 1. The device checks the crc. It refuses with ERR,SCHED_REJECTED if the crc is wrong or any line failed, and nothing changes. 2. Outside a run, the schedule goes to NEXT.TXT and takes effect at the next RUN:BEGIN. The device keeps running what it was running. 3. During a run, the schedule replaces SCHED.TXT straight away. The device keeps its phase number and phase start time, and re-checks the UNTIL conditions immediately. - <phase> is the phase FNT believes the device is in. If the device has moved on in the meantime, the commit is refused with ERR,SCHED_STALE; FNT re-checks the edit and sends it again. 4. A partial upload is discarded 10 s after its last line.

RUN:BEGIN 1. The device refuses with ERR,RUN_SCHED unless its pending schedule (or, if none is pending, its schedule in force) has crc <crc>. That guarantees the run starts on the schedule FNT expects. 2. If a run is already active, the device ends it first (run_end in the old file). 3. It promotes NEXT.TXT, zeroes all counters, opens <run id>.CSV, logs run_start, and enters phase 0 with t0 as its start time.

Run ids are 8 characters, so file names stay valid on any FAT card.

docs.title: Device → host
docs.text:
Line When ROW,<SD row> Every row written to the card, the moment it is written, and again in reply to READ. BOOT,fw=…,reset=<power\|watchdog\|software\|external>,clock=<ok\|unset>,sched=<crc\|default>,run=<id\|-> At startup. STATUS,id=,fw=,time=,clock=ok\|unset,sd=ok\|err,run=,ended=0\|1,sched=,next_sched=,phase=,phase_name=,phase_start=,next=,file=,seq=,l=,r=,pellets=,phase_rewards=,phase_left=,phase_right=,depleted=0\|1,well=0\|1,jam=0\|1,uptime=,batt=,temp=,hum=,lights=0\|1 In reply to STATUS. sched and next_sched are crcs (- if none). next describes the soonest UNTIL, for example at=2026-10-20T19:00-07:00 or rewards=37/100. ERR,<code>,<detail> Bad command or bad value, or an SD write failure (ERR,SD,…).

crc is CRC-32 (the zlib.crc32 polynomial) of the schedule's lines, each ending in \n. FNT compiles the same text, so a single number shows whether a device holds the schedule FNT expects.

docs.title: Data file
docs.text:
One file per run, with this header:

time,ms,seq,phase,event,side,outcome,left,right,pellets,phase_rewards,phase_left,phase_right,retrieval_ms,poke_ms,detail
Column Meaning time ISO 8601 with UTC offset, to the second (RTC resolution). Blank while clock=unset. ms millis(), for ordering and intervals within a second. It wraps after 49.7 days, so only differences between nearby rows mean anything. seq Monotonic within a run, starting at 1. phase The phase number when the row was written. event poke, dispense (a pellet reached the well), retrieve, jam, phase, schedule, run_start, run_end, boot, clock, status, error. side, outcome For pokes. side is L or R. outcome is reward, counted, inactive, timeout, short, pellet_in_well or depleted. left, right, pellets Totals for the run. phase_rewards, phase_left, phase_right Totals for the phase, which UNTIL and the quota use. retrieval_ms On retrieve rows: the time from dispense to retrieval, however long it was. Nothing times out; the row is written whenever the well clears. poke_ms On poke rows: how long the beam was broken. detail ;-separated, never commas. phase: the name, plus ;goto or ;catch-up;start=<iso>. dispense: free, manual or retry (blank for a reward). jam: what was being dispensed. boot: reset=<cause>;ratio counters reset. clock: from=<iso>;to=<iso>. run_start: t0=<iso>;<first phase>. status (hourly): batt=…;temp=…;hum=…. poke: held if the beam stayed broken past 60 s.

docs.title: Firmware changes needed to keep these promises
docs.text:
• Hardware watchdog, with every wait bounded well below its period. The library's logLeftPoke, logRightPoke and RotateDisk contain unbounded while (beam broken) loops and are replaced. The watchdog is also fed during the boot-time back-scan.
  • Jam handling: a bounded number of attempts, then a jam row, then a retry every 10 minutes rather than giving up for good.
  • SD failure: if the card can't be read, the device stays in the current phase (it can't read the next one), keeps running, reports sd=err, and retries.
  • Output: whole lines go out with Serial.write(buf, len), with no if (Serial) checks, which cost 10 ms each.
  • SD: the card is initialised once at boot instead of on every row, and there is no 100 ms LED blink per row.
  • Display: shows the phase name, the counts and the next change, and is redrawn on change only.
  • LEDs: turned off and the motor-driver enable line released after every flash.
  • Removed: the 14 modes, the MODE/NEW_TRIAL/SYNC/LIGHTS/file-transfer commands, the event queue, the pending-command slot, the boot ID menu and start.csv/stop.csv.

docs.title: Part 4: protocol files
docs.text: A protocol is a YAML file. It is what the FNT editor writes, what a methods section can quote, and what the tests run without hardware. FNT compiles it into one schedule per device and stores the file, with its hash, in every run folder.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
format: fnt-fed3-protocol/2
name: Short name
description: Free text.
devices: [FED001, FED002]   # FED3 IDs: the same name on the device, in data and in FNT

colors:                  # optional; added to the built-in names
  amber: [30, 10, 0, 0]

cues:                    # optional named cues
  reward_flash:
    - tone: {hz: 4000, ms: 200}
    - flash: {target: bar, color: blue, ms: 500}

rules:                   # optional named rules
  base:
    active: both
    cue: {reward: reward_flash}
  rich: {use: base, quota: 30, quota_period: 1h}

phases:                  # run in order; the last one runs until Stop
  - name: …
    until: …             # when this phase ends (omit on the last phase)
    rule: …              # the rule every device runs
    only: {FED002: …}    # changes to the rule for some devices
    rotate: …            # reassign rules between devices periodically
    daily: […]           # clock-time windows inside this phase

checks:                  # optional; what the GUI flags as a problem
  no_pellets: 8h

devices means one thing: the list of FED3s at the top. Every device in it runs every phase, so a phase's rule is what they all do; only changes it for the devices it names.

docs.title: Rules in the file
docs.text:
A rule is either a mapping of the keys from Part 1, or the name of an entry in rules. use: <name> inside a mapping starts from that named rule; the keys written beside it override it.

only (in a phase or a daily window) maps FED3s to rules. A key can name several FED3s, separated by commas, to give them one rule:

rule: {active: both, ratio: 1}
only:
  FED001, FED002: {ratio: 5}        # FR5 on both pokes, for these two
  FED003: {active: left}            # FR1 on the left poke

Each FED3 may appear in only once. Inside { } a comma separates entries, so there a key naming several FED3s needs quotes, {"FED001, FED002": rich}, or is written as a list, {[FED001, FED002]: rich}. A phase with only and no rule runs the defaults (FR1 on the left poke) on the devices only leaves out, which the checker warns about.

cue.* keys are written as a nested cue: mapping. A cue is a named cue, or a list of actions where each action is either a one-key mapping or click:

cue:
  reward:
    - tone: {hz: 4000, ms: 200}
    - flash: {target: poke, color: green, ms: 300}
  counted: [click]
  timeout:
    - noise: {ms: 300}
  depleted:
    - bnc: {width: 10, hz: 1, count: 1}

Built-in colours: white (0:0:0:40), red (30:0:0:0), green (0:30:0:0) and blue (0:0:30:0). Colours can also be written as [r, g, b, w].

docs.title: Durations, clock times and conditions
docs.text:
• Durations are 90s, 15m, 48h, 10d, or combinations such as 1d12h. The rule keys timeout, quota_period and refill_delay also accept a bare number of seconds. after and every need a unit, so after: 48 can't silently mean 48 seconds.
  • Clock times are "19:00", quoted because YAML would otherwise read 19:00 as the number 1140. They are in standard time (see Clock).

until takes one condition, or a list of conditions where the first one met ends the phase:

Condition Ends the phase Checked by {after: 48h} 48 h after the phase started. Device {at: "19:00"} At the first 19:00 after the phase started. Device {at: "19:00", day: 3} At 19:00 on day 3 of the run. Device {rewards: 200, of: each} On each device by itself, when that device has delivered 200 rewards in this phase. Device {pokes: 500, side: any, of: each} On each device by itself, after 500 pokes on it in this phase (side can be left, right or any). Device {rewards: 200, of: all} On every device at once, when every device has delivered 200 rewards in this phase. FNT {rewards: 200, of: any} On every device at once, when any one device has delivered 200. FNT {rewards: 200, of: [FED001, FED002]} On every device at once, when each one listed has delivered 200. FNT {manual: true} When someone presses Advance phase. FNT

of says whose counts end the phase, and works the same for pokes. With of: each the devices move on separately, so they can end up in different phases. of can be left out when the protocol has one device; with several, the checker warns until it's written, so that a phase never splits the devices up without saying so.

docs.title: Conditions that need FNT
docs.text:
A device only knows its own counts. A condition that depends on other devices, or on a person pressing Advance phase, has to be checked by FNT.

  • How FNT does it: it watches phase_rewards, phase_left and phase_right in each device's live rows. When the condition is met, it sends GOTO:<n>,<n+1> to every device still in phase n. Devices that already left by a local fallback are untouched.
  • If FNT is down, such a phase doesn't end until FNT is back, unless it also has a device-local condition. until: [{rewards: 100, of: all}, {after: 4d}] ends at whichever comes first, and the 4-day limit still applies with FNT down.
  • The checker and editor mark every phase that needs FNT, and warn when it has no device-local fallback.

docs.title: Rotation
docs.text:
rotate reassigns named rules between devices, one period at a time, which covers patch swaps and rich/poor reshuffles:

rotate:
  every: 1d
  at: "19:00"          # optional, and only with every: 1d
  mode: cycle          # cycle: each device takes the next one's assignment
                       # shuffle: random permutation, seeded per run
  assign:              # the first period; every device needs one
    FED001, FED002: rich
    FED003, FED004: poor

assign names devices the same way only does.

FNT expands a rotation into consecutive phases (Competition 1, Competition 2, …), one per period, with each device given its own assignment. The device needs no rotation logic of its own. The shuffle seed is saved in run.json, so the sequence can be reproduced.

A rotating phase lasts a whole number of periods. Its until must be {after: …} and a multiple of every: {after: 14d} with every: 1d means 14 periods. Each expanded phase ends at at=<time>, or at after=<every> if there's no at. Counting periods matters because a rotating phase usually starts when an earlier condition is met, so its start time isn't known when the schedule is compiled. With at, the first period runs only from the phase start to the next boundary.

docs.title: Daily windows
docs.text:
daily:
  - {from: "07:00", to: "19:00", rule: {free_feed: 1}}
  - {from: "20:00", to: "22:00", only: {FED002: {ratio: 3}}}

A window overrides keys from the phase's rule between two clock times every day, for every device (rule), for some (only), or both. A device only leaves out keeps the phase's rule during the window. A window may cross midnight. Windows within a phase may not overlap; this is checked when the file is loaded.

docs.title: Merge order
docs.text:
Each phase's rule for a device is built by merging, in this order (later wins): 1. the built-in defaults; 2. the phase's rule; 3. the phase's rotation assignment for that device; 4. the phase's only entry for that device.

daily windows become WINDOW lines.

docs.title: Format 1
docs.text:
Files written as format: fnt-fed3-protocol/1 still load, so older protocols and runs keep working, but FNT writes format 2. Format 1 used other names for the same three things:

Format 1 Format 2 phase or window all: rule: phase or window devices: {FED001: …} only: {FED001: …} until: {rewards: 100, devices: all} until: {rewards: 100, of: all} until: {rewards: 100} until: {rewards: 100, of: each}

To move a file to format 2, change its first line and these keys. The form in the editor writes whichever format the file it's editing uses.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text: checks.no_pellets flags a device that hasn't dispensed a pellet for that long, while its current rule can dispense (free_feed=1, or reward=pellet with active other than none). The other problems the GUI flags are always on (Part 5).

docs.title: Command-line tools
docs.text:
The compiler that produces the schedules is also available from the command line:

  • fnt-fed check protocol.yaml finds errors with line numbers:
  • unknown keys;
  • out-of-range values;
  • overlapping windows;
  • a phase that can never end;
  • a device name that isn't declared, or one given twice in only or assign;
  • a schedule over the device limits.

It warns about a count condition without of when there are several devices, and a phase whose only leaves devices on the defaults. It also lists the phases that need FNT. - fnt-fed compile protocol.yaml prints each device's schedule. - fnt-fed preview protocol.yaml --days 21 prints the timeline. Count conditions are shown as "after 200 rewards" rather than given times.

docs.title: Part 5: runs
docs.text:
Setup ──Start──▶ Pre-flight ──all pass──▶ Running ──Stop──▶ Stopped
                     │ fail
                     └──▶ back to Setup, with the reason shown on each device

Setup - Choose the protocol and output folder. The protocol names its FED3s by ID, so there's nothing to bind: FED007 is the FED3 whose ID is 7. - Manual FEED and TEST work here for bench checks.

Pre-flight, for each bound device: - it is connected, with proto=3; - clock=ok, and the drift is recorded after setting the clock; - sd=ok; - its compiled schedule uploads to NEXT.TXT, and the crc matches; - optionally, it plays a test cue.

A device that fails blocks Start unless you remove it from the run explicitly.

Start happens at a single instant, t0: - FNT sends RUN:BEGIN,<id>,<t0>,<crc> to every device; - FNT waits for every RUN reply before showing Running; - counters, plot, log and the elapsed clock all start at t0.

Running - FNT polls STATUS, keeps a live copy of the rows and fills any gap with READ. - FNT checks the conditions that need it. - FNT flags problems on screen. - Manual actions are logged with their source.

Editing mid-run 1. Edit the protocol in FNT. 2. FNT checks the edit: - phases before each device's current phase must be unchanged; - the current phase must keep its position, but its rule and conditions may change. 3. FNT recompiles and commits to each device, with the device's current phase (ERR,SCHED_STALE means "re-check and resend"). 4. The change takes effect immediately; elapsed time and counts carry over.

Each version is kept in the run folder (protocol.v2.yaml, …), and run.json records when it took effect.

Stop - FNT sends RUN:END, pulls the remaining rows and writes a summary. - The devices keep running their current phase until the next run, and keep writing rows to the same file. FNT keeps copying them, after the run_end row, until the device starts another run: in the Stopped view, after New run, and after FNT restarts (a device reporting a stopped run that's in the runs folder is picked back up). - A device that missed RUN:END (it was unplugged) is sent it when it's back. - run.json keeps stopped_at (when Stop was pressed, UTC) and ended: for each device, the time, seq and detail of its run_end row, so the rows recorded after Stop can be told apart even when a device ended late or had no clock. - FNT never sends RUN:BEGIN for a run a device reports as ended: the device would start that run's file over. A run left running in run.json whose devices already ended it (FNT closed mid-Stop) is flagged, and Stop finishes it.

Crash recovery: if FNT finds an unfinished run at launch, it resumes it: - it rebinds the devices; - it compares the schedule crcs; - it READs the missing rows.

The devices were never waiting for it.

docs.title: What the GUI flags
docs.text:
There are no external notifications: rooms are checked daily, so a problem only has to be impossible to miss on screen. Each device card shows a problem state, and the run header shows a count of open problems.

A device card flags: - no reply for 2 minutes; - jam; - watchdog reset; - sd=err; - clock=unset; - schedule crc mismatch; - clock drift over 60 s; - the device being in a different run; - checks.no_pellets.

A problem stays flagged until you acknowledge it, even if it has cleared, so an overnight jam is still visible at the morning check.

docs.title: Run folder
docs.text:
2026-10-20_1900_four-patch/
  run.json          # protocol hash, binding, t0 (UTC), clock offset, seed,
                    # edits, FNT-driven phase changes, firmware versions
  protocol.yaml     # exact copy (plus protocol.v2.yaml … after edits)
  sched/FED001.txt  # each device's compiled schedule
  log.csv           # FNT actions, uploads, problems, disconnects (UTC)
  FED001.csv        # byte-identical copy of the device's data file
  P2_FED007.csv
  …

FNT writes each device's copy in seq order, holding rows that arrive early until READ fills the gap. The live view uses rows as they arrive. The copy follows the device's file past run_end (see Stop).

docs.title: Part 6: the GUI
docs.text: The GUI has one job per run state. Everything the devices and FNT can do on their own (clock sync, data copying, port scanning, recovery) has no button.

docs.title: Code layout
docs.text:
fnt/fed3/
  schedule.py     # the device schedule format, limits and timing rules
  protocol.py     # parse, check, compile, preview. Pure Python, no Qt.
  device_sim.py   # a FED3 on firmware v3, simulated: the firmware's spec
  link.py         # one serial port and the v3 line protocol (no threads)
  run.py          # devices, runs, data copies, FNT conditions, problems (no Qt)
  demo.py         # simulated devices for trying the window without hardware
  cli.py          # fnt-fed check | compile | preview
  ui/             # window, setup and running views, editor, plot, log, the FED3 drawing
  • run.py has no widgets and no threads of its own. Everything happens in Engine.step(); the window runs it on one background thread, sends it commands through a queue and reads snapshots. The tests drive step() directly against simulated devices on a simulated clock.
  • Separate process: the FED3 window is a launcher tool like the others (fnt.tool_launcher, key fed3), so a crash takes down only the window, and the devices don't notice either way.
  • Demo mode: python -m fnt.fed3.ui.window --demo 4 --speed 60 opens the window with four simulated FED3s and an animal poking at each, a minute per second.

docs.text:
┌ 1 Setup › 2 Running › 3 Stopped  Four-patch competition · 3 of its 4 FED3s plugged in┐
├ Protocol ───────────────────────┬ FED3s ────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ four-patch.yaml [Open][New][Edit]│ This protocol uses FED001, FED002, FED003,    │
│ ✓ 17 phases · 4 devices          │ FED004.                                       │
│ ┌ Timeline ────────────────────┐ │ Port ID           Status             Tests    │
│ │ 1 Habituation                │ │ COM3 [ FED001 ]   SD ok              [L][T][F]│
│ │   ends at 19:00 on day 3     │ │ COM4 [ FED002 ]   SD ok              [L][T][F]│
│ │ 2 Training [needs FNT] …     │ │ COM5 [ FED003 ]   SD error           [L][T][F]│
│ └──────────────────────────────┘ │ COM6 [ FED009 ]   not in this protocol        │
│                                  │ FED004 isn't plugged in. Plug in, or give a   │
│                                  │ FED3 that ID.                                 │
├──────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Runs are saved in ~/FED3_Runs                [Change folder] [ Start run ▶ ]    │
│                Not ready: FED004 isn't plugged in. Plug in, or give a FED3 that ID. │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  • Every FED3 plugged in has a row, in port order, and a row stays with its FED3.
  • ID is the FED3's one name, FED001-FED999: on its screen, in the protocol's devices, in its data file (FED007.csv) and on its card. It's kept in DEVICE.TXT and set on the FED3's boot menu, or with ID: from the ID box: type 7, 007 or FED007 and press Enter (or leave the box); anything outside 1-999 is put back. The box isn't refreshed while it has focus, so typing is never overwritten. Firmware starts at 1. Start's binding is simply FED007 -> 7. Two connected FED3s can't share an ID, since data files and the engine find devices by it. The protocol's IDs show in their series colour; a FED3 it doesn't name shows not in this protocol.
  • An ID changed on the FED3 itself shows up in its next STATUS, and FNT follows it.
  • The ID box renumbers the FED3 on that row (ID:); a number another FED3 has swaps them, in one engine command, and Setup says so under the table. The engine refuses to renumber a FED3 in the running run. A FED3 in a stopped run still records into it, and rows are matched to a run's devices by number, so the stopped run follows the new number (run.json keeps binding as it was at Start and lists the change under renumbered).
  • Lights sends LIGHTS:on/off (firmware 3.1), and the button follows the device's lights status.
  • Start runs pre-flight and reports per row, so a failure is shown on the row that caused it. A FED3 in another run that hasn't ended fails pre-flight (an upload would replace that run's schedule in place) unless the person confirms ending it; then FNT sends RUN:END before uploading.

docs.title: Protocol editor
docs.text:
The file is the protocol, so the editor edits the file: - The YAML text on the left. Nothing is converted to and from a form, so comments and layout survive. - A live check on the right, re-run as you type. It uses the same code as fnt-fed check, and clicking a problem jumps to its line. - The timeline below it: when each phase starts and ends, each device's rule, and which phases need FNT. - New from template: each classic FED3 mode (and FNT's FRTO and RR) as a one-phase protocol, as in "What replaces the old modes"; and examples: FR1 on both pokes with a cue, stepping the ratio up by rewards, a four-patch competition. - Add phase…: a form for the common settings (where it goes, end condition, active poke, ratio, timeout, quota, free feeding, pellet or none, reward tone, flash and BNC train, clicks). It writes the YAML for you, so a new phase never needs typing. With several devices, an end on rewards or pokes is labelled "each device on its own" and written with of: each. In a format 1 file the form writes format 1 keys. - Edit phase / Remove phase: the same form, filled from a phase's YAML, or deleting its lines. A phase the form can't show in full (named rules, rotation, windows, per-device rules in only) is edited in the text instead; the form never drops what it can't show. - During a run the editor opens on the running protocol and Apply to running devices sends it. The engine refuses an edit that changes a finished phase or moves a device's current phase.

A form for every construct (rotation, windows, per-device overrides), or a Blockly or node-graph editor, could be added later as other ways to write the same file. Nothing else would change.

  • Device cards, below the plot, in as many columns as fit:
  • the FED3 drawn with left pokes, pellets and right pokes since t0 on it;

docs.title: 1. Both pokes, stepping up the ratio by count
docs.text:
format: fnt-fed3-protocol/2
name: FR1 to FR5, both pokes
devices: [FED001]

cues:
  reward:
    - tone: {hz: 4000, ms: 200}
    - flash: {target: poke, color: blue, ms: 500}

rules:
  base: {active: both, cue: {reward: reward}}

phases:
  - name: FR1
    until: {rewards: 50}
    rule: {use: base, ratio: 1}
  - name: FR3
    until: {rewards: 100}
    rule: {use: base, ratio: 3}
  - name: FR5
    rule: {use: base, ratio: 5}

This compiles to:

NAME FR1 to FR5, both pokes
PHASE FR1
UNTIL rewards=50
SET active=both cue.reward=tone:4000:200+flash:poke:0:0:30:0:500
PHASE FR3
UNTIL rewards=100
SET active=both ratio=3 cue.reward=tone:4000:200+flash:poke:0:0:30:0:500
PHASE FR5
SET active=both ratio=5 cue.reward=tone:4000:200+flash:poke:0:0:30:0:500

docs.title: 2. Four-patch competition with depletion and daily reshuffle
docs.text:
format: fnt-fed3-protocol/2
name: Four-patch competition
description: >
  Two rich and two poor patches that each refill hourly. Which patches are
  rich is reshuffled every day at lights-off.
devices: [FED001, FED002, FED003, FED004]

cues:
  reward:
    - tone: {hz: 4000, ms: 200}
    - flash: {target: bar, color: green, ms: 1000}

rules:
  patch:
    active: both
    cue: {reward: reward, depleted: [click]}
  rich: {use: patch, ratio: 1, quota: 30, quota_period: 1h}
  poor: {use: patch, ratio: 5, quota: 10, quota_period: 1h}

phases:
  - name: Habituation
    until: {at: "19:00", day: 3}
    rule: {active: none, free_feed: 1}

  - name: Training
    until: [{rewards: 100, of: all}, {after: 4d}]
    rule: patch

  - name: Competition
    until: {after: 14d}
    rotate:
      every: 1d
      at: "19:00"
      mode: shuffle
      assign:
        FED001, FED002: rich
        FED003, FED004: poor

  - name: Recovery
    rule: {active: none, free_feed: 1}

checks:
  no_pellets: 8h

Training is the only phase that needs FNT, and it falls back to 4 days on its own. Each device's schedule has 17 phases: Habituation, Training, Competition 1–14 and Recovery. Every Competition phase ends at the next 19:00, so the first one is short unless Training happens to end at 19:00.

docs.title: 3. Timed feeding
docs.text:
format: fnt-fed3-protocol/2
name: Timed feeding 19:00-21:00
devices: [FED001]
phases:
  - name: Restricted
    rule: {active: none}
    daily:
      - {from: "19:00", to: "21:00", rule: {free_feed: 1}}

The window runs on the device, so it opens and closes on time with the PC off. It also keeps working after Stop.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text: Question Decision Legacy FED3 compatibility None: new modes, commands and file format. Lights Off unless a cue flashes them. Both pokes One shared counter by default; count=per_port is a setting. Clock Standard time all year, matching a vivarium that ignores daylight saving. Blank card FR1, left poke. After Stop The device keeps running its current phase, including daily windows. Where the schedule runs On the device; FNT only checks conditions that span devices. Several devices in a phase One rule for all of them, only for exceptions, and of on a count condition saying whose counts end it (format 2). Notifications None. The GUI flags problems until they're acknowledged. status rows Hourly. Limits 256 phases, 8 daily windows and 6 until lines per phase. Mid-run edits to the current phase Take effect immediately.

docs.title: Running FED3 experiments
docs.text:
[!WARNING] Alpha. This works end to end against simulated devices and the firmware's logic built for a PC. It has not yet been run on FED3 hardware; see the bench checklist in the fnt-fed3 README first.

The FED3s run the experiment themselves. FNT writes the protocol, starts the run, keeps a copy of the data, and shows you what each device is doing. If the PC crashes, reboots or is unplugged, the devices carry on; reopen FED3 in FNT and it picks the run back up.

docs.title: Before the first run
docs.text:
1. Flash every FED3 with firmware v3 (fnt-fed3; 3.1 adds Lights).
  2. Devices on older firmware show up in FED3 with a warning and aren't used.
  3. On 3.0 everything works except Lights.
  4. Give each one its own ID. A FED3's ID is its one name: on its screen, in your protocols, in its data file and on FNT's screens, e.g. FED007. A newly flashed FED3 is FED001. Set it either way; it's kept on the SD card, so it's a one-time job:
  5. On the FED3: power it on, and while the screen shows FED3 ID, hold both pokes for a second. Left poke −1, right poke +1 (hold to go faster). It saves after 4 seconds without a poke. (Not offered during a run.)
  6. In FNT: FNT → FED → FED3, then type the ID in the ID box on that FED3's row in Setup and press Enter: 7, 007 or FED007, any number from 1 to 999. Lights shows which FED3 a row is.

docs.title: Writing a protocol
docs.text:
A protocol is a short YAML file: the FED3s it uses, by ID (devices: [FED001, FED002]), and phases, each with a rule and a way to end.

  • Start from a template. In Setup, New… opens the editor; New from template has:
  • Classic FED3 modes, one protocol each: Free feeding, FR1, FR3, FR5, Progressive ratio, Extinction, FR1 and PR reversed (right poke), Optogenetic stimulation and its reversed version, Timed feeding, and FNT's FR with timeout and Random ratio. They keep the classic 4 kHz tone and blue light on a reward, and the click on pokes that don't earn one. Light tracking isn't available: it needs a poke light that stays on.
  • Examples: FR1 on both pokes, stepping the ratio up, a four-patch competition.
  • Add phase… writes a phase from a form: where it goes, when it ends, which poke is active, the ratio, timeout, quota, free feeding, whether a reward delivers a pellet, a tone, flash or BNC pulses on rewards, and clicks.
  • The form switches off whatever can't apply. Free feeding means no active poke, so the ratio, reward and cues go grey; with no active poke a phase can't end on rewards. A click needs what it marks: a timeout, a quota, or a ratio above 1.
  • The check catches the same things in text: a phase that only ends on rewards no poke can earn is an error, and free feeding with an active poke is a warning.
  • Edit phase reads a phase back into the same form and rewrites it, and Remove phase deletes one. A phase that uses something the form doesn't have (a named rule, a rotation, daily windows, per-device rules in only) is edited in the text: the form says what it can't show and takes you to the phase rather than drop it. Comments inside a phase the form rewrites are lost.
  • With several FED3s, every one runs every phase. A phase's rule is what they all do, and only changes it for the ones it names:
- name: Training
  until: {rewards: 100, of: all}
  rule: {active: both, ratio: 1}
  only:
    FED003, FED004: {ratio: 5}

of says whose rewards end the phase: all moves every FED3 on together once each has 100 (FNT checks this, so it must be running), and each moves each FED3 on by itself when it reaches 100. With several FED3s the check warns until you write one. - Older protocols (format: fnt-fed3-protocol/1) still open and run. They used all for rule, and devices for both only and of; see design.md. - The check on the right updates as you type and points at the line of any problem. - The timeline below it shows when each phase will start, and marks the phases that need FNT running to end. - The full format is in design.md, Part 4. The command line checks files too:

fnt-fed check protocol.yaml
fnt-fed preview protocol.yaml --days 21
fnt-fed compile protocol.yaml        # the text each device receives

Times of day are in standard time all year, the time your vivarium's lights keep. In summer, "19:00" is 20:00 on a wall clock that follows daylight saving. FNT labels every time it shows with its zone.

docs.title: Starting a run
docs.text:
Setup has the protocol and its timeline on the left, and every FED3 plugged in on the right, one row each in port order: Port, ID, Status, and Tests (Lights, Tone, Feed). A row always shows the same FED3. The bar across the top says how many of the protocol's FED3s are plugged in.

  1. Choose the protocol (Open…).
  2. Plug in the FED3s it names. Setup lists them (This protocol uses FED001, FED002) and shows their IDs in the colour each has on the cards and plot. A FED3 the protocol doesn't name shows not in this protocol and isn't used.
  3. If one is missing, Setup says so (FED004 isn't plugged in). Plug it in, or type that ID in another FED3's ID box.
  4. Typing an ID another FED3 has swaps the two, and Setup says so. Two FED3s can't share an ID, because their data files are named by it.
  5. A FED3 can't be renumbered during a run. After Stop it can: the stopped run's copy keeps following it under its new number, and run.json records the change.
  6. Lights lights a FED3's bar and pokes white until you press it again, so you can see which is which. They go dark when the run starts.
  7. The status column shows whether the device is ready: clock, SD card and firmware.
  8. Tone plays the protocol's reward tone, and Feed dispenses a pellet. With an empty hopper a dispense sounds like rhythmic beeping with bursts: that's the motor working through its jam-clearing turns for about a minute, then a jam row and a retry every 10 minutes.
  9. Press Start run.
  10. FNT checks every device first: connected, clock set, SD card working, schedule uploaded.
  11. If any device fails, nothing starts and the reason shows on that device's row.
  12. Otherwise every device starts at the same moment.
  13. A FED3 still in a run that was never stopped (its row says still in run …) isn't started over without asking. This happens when FNT couldn't pick that run back up, for example because it was saved in another folder. Start names the FED3s and the run and asks: Cancel, then Change folder… to that run's folder, to keep it going; End it and start ends it on those FED3s first.
  14. FED3s still recording into a stopped run are listed under the table; starting a new run on them ends that.

Runs are saved in Documents/FED3_Runs unless you choose another folder. Runs in folders used before are still followed: a stopped run keeps copying, and an unfinished one is picked back up. If FNT can't read or load one, it says so in Setup instead of failing to open.

docs.title: During a run
docs.text:
The bar across the top of the window shows where you are: Setup › Running › Stopped, with a note on the current step.

  • Each device's card shows:
  • the FED3 drawn with its left pokes, pellets and right pokes on it, each flashing as it goes up (dimmed while the device isn't connected);
  • beside it, its current phase and rule, rewards this phase, when the phase ends, its last event, and its port, battery and temperature;
  • any problem: a jam, offline, a watchdog restart, a dead SD card, a clock that's wrong, no pellets for too long, or the wrong schedule.

A problem stays on the card, outlined in red, until you press Acknowledge, even if it has cleared, so an overnight jam is still visible in the morning. - Feed on a card dispenses a pellet by hand (recorded as manual: a pellet, not a reward). More ▾ has Play a cue… and Set its clock now…, which sets the clock even across a big jump, after asking. - The counts on the drawing are left pokes, pellets and right pokes, as labelled under it. - The plot runs across the top at full width: cumulative pellets per device, with phase changes dotted and Stop dashed. The menu in its title draws the time axis in standard time (as the devices keep it), local time with daylight saving, or UTC. The cards flow below it in as many columns as fit. - Temperature and humidity show only on a FED3 fitted with an AHT20 sensor; without one the device reports nan and the card leaves them out. - The log runs along the bottom of the window, newest last: problems in red, phase changes in blue, run starts and stops in green, and things people did in purple. ▼ Log collapses it to its header, which then counts what's new. - Edit protocol… changes the protocol mid-run. - Phases already over can't change. - The current phase can, and the change applies at once. - The editor says as you type if the running devices can't take an edit, and won't apply it. If one moves on to the next phase while you're editing and the edit no longer fits, FNT says so and reopens the editor with your changes. - A FED3 that's unplugged when you apply gets the edit when it's back. - Each version is kept in the run folder. - Phases FNT moves (counts across devices, or by hand): a FED3 that's unplugged at that moment is moved on as soon as it's back. - Advance phase appears only when the current phase ends by hand. - Closing the window doesn't stop the run. The devices keep running and recording to their SD cards; when you reopen FED3, FNT copies what it missed.

docs.title: Stopping
docs.text:
Stop run ends the run: phases stop changing. Each device keeps running its current phase, including any daily feeding window, until the next run starts, so stopping never cuts the animals off.

The devices also keep recording. Their rows after Stop go to the same file on the card, and FNT keeps copying them into the run's folder (after a run_end row) until the device starts another run: in the Stopped view, after New run, and after FNT is reopened. A device that was unplugged when you pressed Stop is stopped as soon as it's back.

To separate the experiment from what came after it: - In each data file, the run_end row is the stop, stamped by the device: every row after it (by seq) was recorded after Stop. - In run.json, stopped_at is when Stop was pressed (UTC), and ended gives each device's run_end row: its time and seq. A device that was unplugged at Stop ends later than stopped_at, and its entry shows when. If a device's clock was lost at that moment its time is empty, and seq still marks the point.

docs.title: What's in a run folder
docs.text:
File run.json The run: protocol hash, which FED3 played which device, start time, rotation seed, edits, phase changes FNT made (with any device that missed one, under missed, until it's caught up), when Stop was pressed (stopped_at), where each device's data after Stop begins (ended), and any FED3 renumbered after Stop (renumbered). protocol.yaml The protocol exactly as started, plus protocol.v2.yaml and so on after edits. sched/FED<nnn>.txt What each FED3 was sent. FED<nnn>.csv A byte-identical copy of that FED3's data file for the run, including what it recorded after Stop. log.csv Everything FNT did and noticed, in UTC.

The data columns are described in design.md, Part 3.

docs.title: Trying it without hardware
docs.text:
python -m fnt.fed3.ui.window --demo 4 --speed 60

This opens FED3 with four simulated devices and a simulated animal poking at each, with a minute passing every second. It uses a separate settings store and saves runs under FED3_Runs/demo.

docs.title: Exporting tables
docs.text:
File ▸ Export… writes folder-wide tables from the .mad files beside your recordings: one row per recording, one row per detection and one row per labelled call, all in one output folder. They are meant for analysis in R or pandas. mad export writes the same tables from the command line, with the same options.

This is different from File ▸ Export Annotations to CSV…, which writes one <recording>_FNT_MAD_annotations.csv beside each wav. Use that one to look at a single recording; use Export… to analyse a run.

docs.title: What it writes
docs.text:
File One row per Contents mad_recordings.csv recording whose last inference was the chosen model where it is, its start time and channel when the file name gives them, its duration, the model and when it ran, its detection and call counts mad_detections.csv detection of those recordings onset, score, review status, harmonic number, contour measures of its mask, brightness ridge mad_labelled_calls.csv labelled (accepted) call, from any model or painted by hand onset and offset, frequency box, MAD's call metrics recomputed from the audio, contour measures, brightness ridge, note and tags mad_call_images/<id>.png labelled call the call and 10 ms either side, every frequency bin (highest at the top); grey = level as MAD stores it, alpha = the call's own mask mad_export.json — how and when each table was last written (model, settings, inputs, FNT version)

The columns are generic. Anything particular to your experiment — trial, treatment, which animals were present, which zone a microphone covers — is not in the tables; join it in your analysis code, by folder, recording, channel or start.

Detections are the model's output: each row is the detection's mask as the model drew it, whatever its review status. Labelled calls are the reviewed masks, including edits and hand-painted calls.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Meaning Recordings The open project's recordings (the Audio list's with no project open), or folders, each searched to the bottom. Only recordings with a .mad file are exported; a recording whose wav has moved is still exported from its .mad. Output folder Where the tables go. Created if needed. Recordings and detections mad_recordings.csv and mad_detections.csv. No audio is read. Model Only recordings whose last inference was this model. The default is the model that analysed the most recordings; the list shows how many each model analysed. Labelled calls are not filtered by model. Labelled calls mad_labelled_calls.csv. Each labelled recording's audio is read to compute the call metrics, so this is the slow table. If the audio is missing the rows are written with those columns blank. Spectrogram images mad_call_images/, one PNG per labelled call. Implies Labelled calls. Include harmonics Off (the default): fundamentals only, i.e. calls whose harmonic_n is blank or 1. On: every detection and labelled call. Skip recordings unchanged since the last export On (the default): see below. Leave out .mad files written in the last N min Default 10. A .mad that changed this recently may still be open in MAD (an inference run in progress), so it is left out until the next export. A .mad that cannot be opened is left out the same way. Set 0 to include everything.

The export runs in the background and shows its progress. Stop ends it after the current recording; the table being written is discarded and the previous one is kept. Closing the window stops it too.

docs.title: Exporting again
docs.text:
Export into the same folder again and only new and changed recordings are read. The rows of every recording whose .mad has the same modification time as last time are copied from the existing tables, so an export of a run in progress mostly costs the recordings analysed since. A recording whose rows in the old table do not add up to the count in mad_recordings.csv is read again.

Nothing is copied when the settings differ from the last export (another harmonics setting, images turned on or off) or when the table format has changed. Turn Skip recordings unchanged off (--full on the command line) after updating FNT, so every value is computed with the current code.

Each table is written to a temporary file and swapped in only when complete, so a crash leaves the previous table as it was.

docs.title: From the command line
docs.text:
# Recordings and detections of the most common model, every .mad under a folder
mad export --input /data/UltrasonicVocalizations_proc --out /data/usv_tables

# Which models analysed which recordings
mad export --input /data/UltrasonicVocalizations_proc --list-models

# A named model (or the unique start of its name), harmonics included
mad export --input /data/UltrasonicVocalizations_proc --out /data/usv_tables \
           --model 20261014_181834 --harmonics

# A project's labelled calls, with their images
mad export --project my_project/ --out /data/usv_tables --labels --images
Flag Meaning --input Folders (searched to the bottom) and/or wav files. --project The recordings registered in a MAD project (with or instead of --input). --out The output folder. --detections mad_recordings.csv and mad_detections.csv. The default when no table is named. --labels mad_labelled_calls.csv. --images mad_call_images/ (implies --labels). --model The model to export; default the most common. --list-models Print each model and its number of recordings, then stop. --harmonics Include harmonics. --full Read every .mad again instead of copying unchanged recordings. --settle-minutes Leave out .mad files written in the last N minutes (default 10).

It prints a line for each step and a progress line every 500 recordings.

docs.title: mad_recordings.csv
docs.text: Column Meaning path Full path of the recording. folder Name of the folder the recording is in. recording File name of the recording. channel Microphone channel from the file name (ch<N>…), when it has one. start Start time from the file name, yyyy-mm-dd HH:MM:SS, when it matches Avisoft's ch<N><yyyy-mm-dd>_<HH-MM-SS>_<n>.wav; otherwise blank. This is the recorder's clock. duration_s Length of the analysed spectrogram, in seconds. model Model of the last inference (its run folder name). inferred_at When that inference ran. threshold Its probability threshold. detections Number of detections, harmonics included. calls Number of detections that are fundamentals (harmonic_n blank or 1). mad_mtime Modification time of the .mad, in seconds since 1970 (UTC). Used by the next export to tell what changed.

docs.title: mad_detections.csv
docs.text:
folder and recording join each row to its recording.

Column Meaning blob_id The detection's id in the .mad. start_s Onset, seconds from the start of the recording (the same time axis as the per-recording CSV). score The model's mean probability over the detection. status pending, accepted or rejected, from the review. harmonic_n, harmonic_call_id Harmonic grouping: 1 is the fundamental, 2 and up its harmonics; the call id groups them. Blank if grouping has not run. contour measures See below. ridge_turns, ridge_rate_hz, ridge_depth_khz, ridge_trill Brightness ridge (mad add-ridge): turns of the brightest continuous path through the mask, half the turns per second of call (Hz), median kHz between successive turns, and 1 for a trill (at least 4 turns at 20 Hz or faster). Blank where the .mad holds no ridge.

docs.title: mad_labelled_calls.csv
docs.text: Column Meaning path, folder, recording, channel As in mad_recordings.csv. rec_start The recording's start time from its file name (as start above). id The label's id in the .mad; also the image's file name. blob_id The detection it was accepted from; blank for a call painted by hand. painted TRUE for a call painted by hand. class Call class. start_s, stop_s Onset and offset, seconds from the start of the recording. min_freq_hz, max_freq_hz The call's frequency box. harmonic_n, harmonic_call_id, f0_hz Harmonic grouping. score, model_name Score and model of the detection it was accepted from. note, tags What the reviewer wrote on the call. peak_freq_hz … aspect_ratio MAD's call metrics, recomputed from the audio, as in the per-recording CSV (see the technical reference). contour measures See below. ridge_* The label's own brightness ridge. image, img_col0, img_col1, f_bin0, f_bin1 The image's file name, and where the call is in it, counted from 1: its first and last columns, and its lowest and highest frequency bins (bin 1 is 0 Hz). Blank without images. mad_mtime As in mad_recordings.csv.

docs.title: Contour measures
docs.text:
Measured from the call's own mask, without the audio. The contour is the mask's mean frequency in each time frame.

Column Meaning duration_ms Width of the mask. f_mean_khz Mean of the contour. f_min_khz, f_max_khz Lowest and highest frequency of the mask. f_start_khz, f_end_khz First and last value of the contour. slope_khz_ms (end − start) / duration. contour_sd_khz Standard deviation of the contour. turns Reversals of the contour by more than one frequency bin. max_jump_khz Largest frame-to-frame change of the contour. thickness_khz Mean height of the mask per time frame. area_px Pixels in the mask.

turns follows the mask's centre and counts small reversals; ridge_turns follows the brightest line inside the mask and counts excursions of at least 3 kHz. A blob-shaped mask over a fast trill has few turns and many ridge_turns.

docs.title: Mask Audio Detector (MAD)
docs.text:
MAD detects and classifies vocalizations using a custom deep-learning pipeline. Rather than hand-tuned DSP thresholds, users label call regions directly on the spectrogram — with the help of a Segment Anything Model — and train a segmentation model that learns to find and classify calls automatically.

Launch from the FNT main GUI Audio tab → Mask Audio Detector (MAD).

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Spectrogram generation — raw audio is converted to a time–frequency spectrogram (short-time Fourier transform) at the recording's native sample rate (up to 250+ kHz).
  • Interactive labeling with SAM2 — the user clicks on a vocalization and a Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2) proposes a pixel-level mask for that call, dramatically accelerating annotation compared to manual painting.
  • Manual refinement — brush and eraser tools correct SAM2 proposals. Labels follow a pending → confirmed / rejected workflow to keep training data clean.
  • Training-data storage — confirmed call masks are stored as rasterized examples in a shared HDF5 store, paired with the corresponding spectrogram patches.
  • Semantic segmentation model — labeled examples train a U-Net (ResNet18 encoder, via segmentation-models-pytorch) to perform pixel-level call detection on spectrograms.
  • Batch inference — the trained model runs across recordings, producing per-pixel prediction masks that are thresholded and converted to discrete call detections with time, frequency, duration, and class metadata.
  • Iterative refinement — predictions are reviewed in the GUI, where the user confirms or corrects them, feeding new examples back into the training set.

docs.title: Project structure
docs.text:
MAD follows SLEAP's project model: a project points at recordings where they already live, the way a SLEAP project points at videos. The project folder holds those path references, the training-data store, and trained model checkpoints — never copies of your audio, which for 250 kHz recordings would run to hundreds of MB per file. Detections are saved in a .mad file next to each recording.

There is a single Audio list: every recording the project knows about. Anything you confirm in it trains the model — there is no separate training set to curate. Large production runs stay outside the list via the Folder inference target, so recordings you are not curating never join the training set.

A project is optional until you train. You can add wavs, label them, load a model from any trained project, run inference and review the results with no project open — labels and detections save beside the audio either way. Training needs a project, because the model and its example store have to live somewhere.

Because recordings are referenced rather than copied, a recording that moves is a soft state: the row is flagged, but training, the example store and every saved detection keep working, and File ▸ Locate Missing Recordings… repoints a whole moved tree from one file. File ▸ Pack Project is the escape hatch — it copies the audio in, making the project self-contained for archiving or sharing.

docs.title: Detection output
docs.text: Each recording's masks, detections and review status live in its <recording>_FNT.mad file beside the wav. File ▸ Export Annotations to CSV… turns that into a standalone <recording>_FNT_MAD_annotations.csv per recording — the same per-file profile SLEAP and DeepLabCut use for video. For analysis across a run, File ▸ Export… (or mad export) writes folder-wide tables instead: one row per recording, one per detection and one per labelled call, with optional spectrogram images of the labelled calls. See Exporting tables. There is no interchange export: third-party formats (Raven, Audacity) are upkeep the project does not carry. If a downstream tool is ever needed, compatibility gets built then.

docs.title: Consecutive-detection merging
docs.text: A long call can surface as several adjacent blobs — split across inference tile seams or broken by a brief sub-threshold dip. Optional consecutive merging stitches these back into one detection: blobs that are close enough in time (and, by default, overlap in frequency) are combined into a single call with a union bounding box and an area-weighted confidence. The frequency-overlap gate keeps calls that are adjacent in time but separated in frequency — such as a harmonic and its fundamental — distinct. Enable it via the CLI (--merge-consecutive) or the MADInferenceConfig.merge_consecutive flag.

docs.title: Command-line interface
docs.text:
MAD's train / analyze / embeddings pipeline is also available headless as the mad console script, for scripting into batch and HPC workflows:

# Run a trained model over a folder (recursive), merging split calls
mad analyze --model weights.pt --input recordings/ --merge-consecutive

# Train a model from a MAD project directory
mad train --project my_project/ --epochs 30 --device cuda

# Export per-detection embeddings for clustering / similarity analysis
mad embeddings --model weights.pt --input recordings/ --out embeddings.npz

# Folder-wide tables of recordings and detections (see Exporting tables)
mad export --input recordings/ --out tables/

# Add stored spectrograms, then brightness ridges, to existing .mad files
mad add-specs --input recordings/
mad add-ridge --input recordings/ --model <project>/models/<run>

# Flag running-wheel squeaks among the stored detections
mad wheel --input recordings/ --workers 3 --low-priority

# Inference with only its progress window on screen; it quits when the run ends
python -m fnt.usv.mad_pyqt --project my_project/ --infer <project>/models/<run> --inference-window-only
# ...and stop that run from the command line: it finishes the current file and quits, no prompt
mad stop --project my_project/

Run mad <command> --help for the full option list. A run started again on the same project skips the recordings it already analysed at the same settings.

docs.title: Running-wheel squeaks
docs.text:
A running wheel near a microphone thumps in the low register (2-15 kHz) at a steady beat, about 7 per second, while a mouse runs. It can also squeak in the upper register, and the model can take those squeaks for calls. They are short and narrow, often near 105 kHz but also lower, and they come back at the thump beat. mad wheel finds them from the audio alone; no video is needed.

For each detection it looks at 2 s of audio either side:

  1. The beat is the autocorrelation peak of the 2-15 kHz energy between 2 and 20 Hz. It takes the shortest strong lag, so a subharmonic (3 beats) is not taken for the beat.
  2. The comb of a band is how much its autocorrelation peaks at 1, 2 and 3 beats and dips half-way between them. The rule computes it for the low band, and for the band of the detection's own mask.
  3. A detection is flagged when all of these hold:
    • the low band's comb is at least 0.15 (the wheel beats cleanly);
    • its own band's comb is at least 0.25;
    • the low band's autocorrelation at the beat is at least 0.2;
    • it is shorter than 0.6 of a beat.

A mouse can call while it runs, so running alone flags nothing. A call that lasts several beats, or a bout with its own rhythm, does not comb at the wheel's beat and is kept. Requiring the low band's own comb keeps dense call bouts: at about 8 calls per second they are close to the wheel's rhythm, but the mouse's own movement noise has no clean beat.

The rule was calibrated on the 2021_8x8 labels. It flagged:

  • 1 of 1,515 accepted calls;
  • 40 % of rejected C57 detections;
  • 75 % of a hand-checked squeak train.

The results go to /wheel in each .mad, and nothing else in the file changes. /wheel holds:

  • one row per detection: blob_id, squeak (0/1), comb, low_comb, period_s, low_acf and dur_beats;
  • a running track in 4-s windows every 0.5 s: track_t_s, track_period_s, track_acf, track_comb and track_running.

A recording is redone automatically after a new inference run. Detections are never deleted. To leave squeaks out of an analysis, drop the rows with squeak = 1.

docs.title: Call embeddings
docs.text: The embeddings command extracts a fixed-length feature vector for each saved detection by pushing its spectrogram patch through the trained model's encoder and global-average-pooling the deepest feature map (512 dimensions for a ResNet18 encoder). The output .npz holds the embeddings alongside each call's source file, id, time bounds, and class — ready for clustering calls by similarity, surfacing novel call types, or comparing repertoires across animals.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• FFmpeg — required for ADPCM and other non-PCM WAV formats. See Installation.
  • PyTorch — required for model training and inference; a CUDA-capable GPU is strongly recommended. See GPU Support.

docs.title: MAD Workflow — from a new project to a finished batch
docs.text:
This is the practical, step-by-step path. It says what to click and why, and where the traps are. For how the pieces work (storage layout, the CSV columns, the normalization rule, resume semantics) see the technical reference in fnt/usv/usv_detector/MAD_README.md.

The loop you are running, end to end:

label a few calls → train → run on your labeled files → accept/reject
       ↑                                                       │
       └──── add breadth, retrain ◄──── evaluate ◄─────────────┘
